comments.body:
# VERDICT: (a) TRUE POSITIVES. All firings are `bound-exceeded`. The drain check is HEALTHY.

AC1 is now satisfied — read directly from `journalctl -u rebar-autodeploy` on
i-00880b2c7f13527c5 via SSM RunShellScript (read-only; no mutation, no config change).

## The reason field behind every firing

    2026-08-07T11:29:23Z  bound-exceeded  in_flight=2  deferred_for=1806s  bound=1800s
    2026-08-07T12:50:04Z  bound-exceeded  in_flight=2  deferred_for=1929s  bound=1800s
    2026-08-12T03:03:04Z  bound-exceeded  in_flight=2  deferred_for=1810s  bound=1800s
    2026-08-12T03:59:33Z  bound-exceeded  in_flight=1  deferred_for=1820s  bound=1800s

**`signal-unavailable` does not appear even once**, in the entire journal back to
2026-07-03. So the branch this ticket correctly flagged as the alarming reading — "the
/health in_flight probe is inert and every deploy has been running blind, a silent
regression of 34cd" — is **ruled out**. AC2 is not applicable; the probe works.

The ticket's circumstantial inference from the deferral run-up was right.

## There is a FOURTH firing this ticket does not list

`2026-08-12T03:59:33Z` (= 2026-08-11 20:59 PDT). The sweep window closed at
2026-08-12T04:00Z and this landed 27 seconds inside it, so it was missed. It is
**4 firings in 7 days**, not 3 — and the 4th came ~56 minutes after the 3rd, i.e. a
second full 1800s bound was spent back-to-back with the first.

## Metric-artifact false positive: checked and EXCLUDED

Worth recording since it was the leading alternative hypothesis. `observability.sh`
§4e counts markers by grepping the WHOLE unit journal cumulatively and publishing
`total - prev`, with `[ "$new" -lt 0 ] && new=$total`. If journald ever vacuumed the
unit's history, `total` would drop below the stored offset and that guard would
re-publish the entire remaining count as "new this interval" — spuriously re-firing a
1-datapoint, threshold-`>0` alarm on history that had already been counted.

Measured on the box: journal total = **7**, offset file
`/var/lib/rebar/autodeploy-interrupt-offset` = **7**, and the unit journal still
reaches back to 2026-07-03T19:50:40Z. No rotation has occurred, offset and total agree
exactly, and every CloudWatch datapoint has a matching journal line at the same minute
(3 on 08-03 pre-fix, 4 post-fix). **No double-count. Every firing is a real, distinct
interrupt.** (The latent rotation hazard is real but has not triggered; filing it
separately rather than conflating it with this ticket.)

## ROOT CAUSE: the bound's rationale assumes serial reviews; the bot runs CONCURRENT ones

This is the part that upgrades the finding from "the bot is busy" to "34cd's bound
argument does not hold". The full deferral episode preceding the 03:03:04 interrupt,
one line per ~2.1-minute tick, unbroken:

    02:32:54  in_flight=2  deferred_for=0s      <- episode opens
    02:35:03  in_flight=2  129s
    02:37:14  in_flight=2  260s
    02:39:24  in_flight=2  390s
    02:41:33  in_flight=2  519s
    02:43:43  in_flight=2  649s
    02:45:54  in_flight=2  780s
    02:48:03  in_flight=1  909s
    02:50:14  in_flight=1  1040s
    02:52:24  in_flight=1  1169s
    02:54:33  in_flight=2  1299s   <- climbs back to 2
    02:56:34  in_flight=2  1420s
    02:58:43  in_flight=2  1549s
    03:00:53  in_flight=2  1679s
    03:03:04  in_flight=2  1810s   -> AUTODEPLOY_REVIEW_INTERRUPT

Every tick deferred; the episode never reset, so the gate behaved exactly as designed.
But look at `in_flight`: it oscillates 2 -> 1 -> 2 and **never reaches 0** across 30
continuous minutes.

34cd justified `DEPLOY_DEFER_MAX=1800` like this (quoting its own implementation note):

> the bot wraps every review in `asyncio.wait_for(..., REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)` on both
> paths (default 1200s), so no single review can outlive that and **in_flight
> necessarily reaches 0 within it**. 1800s is 1.5x that ceiling [...] so the bound is
> only reachable by a CHRONICALLY busy bot, never by one ordinary review.

The premise is true per-review and false in aggregate. `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` bounds
each review's lifetime, but `in_flight` is a **concurrent gauge**: with two reviews
overlapping and new ones arriving as old ones finish, the counter is refilled before it
can drain, so the idle window the bound waits for never opens. No review outlived 1200s
here — the trace shows completions (2->1) throughout. The bound is not being defeated by
a stuck review; it is being outlasted by ordinary pipelining.

So "reachable only by a chronically busy bot" is accurate as written, but the implied
rarity does not follow: **any landing burst that sustains >=1 concurrent review for 30
minutes spends the bound**, and at present cadence that is roughly weekly, twice in one
hour on 2026-08-11. The exceptional case has become routine because the reasoning
treated a concurrency gauge as if it were a single-review timer.

## STOPPING HERE — the remedy is an operator decision, not a behavior-preserving fix

Per the bug-bash brief I stop at diagnosis when the fix would change autodeploy or
review behavior. Every candidate does:

- **Raise `DEPLOY_DEFER_MAX`.** Trades a killed review for a longer deploy stall, and
  34cd deliberately pinned it to 1.5x `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` with a test asserting
  `bound >= REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`. Note the trace shows raising it alone may not even
  work: the episode was saturated, so a larger bound just defers the same kill. This
  ticket was right to flag it as the wrong reflex.
- **Cap review concurrency**, so `in_flight` can actually reach 0. Changes review
  throughput.
- **Accept it** (AC3) and treat interrupts as ordinary burst residue — which then argues
  the alarm should not be a 1-datapoint pager.

My recommendation, for whoever takes the decision: this is **not an outage** — the
reconciler retries each killed review, and no `signal-unavailable` means the drain check
is doing its job on every other tick. But the alarm is currently paging on a condition
that is now normal-cadence, so the real choice is between accepting the interrupts and
retuning the alarm, versus making `in_flight` drainable. I would not raise the bound.

## AC4 remains genuinely open and is the one cheap, low-risk piece

`rebar/host:review_interrupts` is dimensionless, which is why this ticket had to hedge
between two readings with opposite fixes and why confirming it needed host shell access
at all. Splitting the two reasons into distinct countable tokens/metrics (or adding a
reason dimension) would let a future sweep read the answer straight from CloudWatch.
That is observability-only and does not touch deploy or review behavior — but it is a
Terraform alarm-contract change requiring an apply, so I am leaving it for the operator
to sequence with whatever AC3 decides, rather than landing it ahead of that decision.

## Method note

Read-only throughout: `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics`, and SSM RunShellScript
issuing only `journalctl`/`cat`/`grep`. Nothing on the box or in AWS was modified, and
no code was changed.

comments.body:
# CLOSING — diagnosis complete, no action on autodeploy behaviour

Operator disposition, 2026-08-12: **accept the current behaviour.** Recorded here so the
reasoning survives the close.

## What was decided

- **No change to `DEPLOY_DEFER_MAX` or to autodeploy's drain gate.** All four firings are
  genuine `bound-exceeded` events, the drain check is healthy (`signal-unavailable` never
  occurred), and interrupted reviews are retried by the backfill reconciler — so this is a
  correctly-functioning alarm on real events, not an outage. 34cd deliberately pinned the bound
  to 1.5x `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` under a test, and the saturated episode trace indicates a
  larger bound would only defer the same kill rather than prevent it.
- **Alarm retune: NOT undertaken.** `rebar-autodeploy-review-interrupts` currently pages on a
  condition now occurring at roughly weekly cadence (twice within one hour on 2026-08-11).
  That is accepted as-is. **Retune only if the pager noise becomes a problem in practice** —
  raising the threshold or the datapoint count today would trade away the fast latch that
  exists specifically so the `signal-unavailable` case cannot hide, and that case is the urgent
  one. Better to keep the sensitivity until noise proves it costly.

## Residue is carried by tickets, not lost in the close

- [rebar:613a-e3f4-14a6-45a3] (dowdy-antarctic-junco) — AC4's dimensionless-metric split, so a
  future CloudWatch-only sweep can distinguish the two reasons without host shell access.
  Observability-only, but a Terraform alarm-contract change needing an operator
  `terraform apply`. Linked `discovered_from`.
- [rebar:2dc7-31b7-ecbb-4cd2] (affluent-conveyable-dromedary) — the latent journal-rotation
  double-count hazard in `observability.sh`'s cumulative marker counters, found and ruled out by
  measurement while excluding a metric artifact as the cause here. Not currently firing. Linked
  `discovered_from`.

## One finding worth carrying forward beyond these tickets

34cd's bound rationale treats `in_flight` as if it were a single-review timer when it is a
concurrent gauge. That reasoning error is now recorded in the description; it is not itself
actionable under the no-action disposition, but it is the reason "reachable only by a
chronically busy bot" understated how often the bound would be spent. Anyone revisiting the
bound should start there rather than from the 1.5x multiplier.

Closing as `not_a_bug`: the system behaved as designed, the alarm fired truthfully, and the
disposition is to accept it. No code was changed; nothing was mutated on the box or in AWS.

No alarm should be tuned for any of them.

A bound raise fixes the true-positive CAUSE rather than loosening a threshold, and would plausibly have prevented all four interrupts (see unskillful-supportive-lion).
- Follow-up pair 23:07Z (rebar-gerrit-voter-errors, rebar-review-bot-merge-change-errors): BOTH FALSE POSITIVES, and the alarms are NOT at fault — the counts were fabricated by probe-side defects in infra/scripts/observability.sh. Nothing was mutated in AWS or on i-00880b2c7f13527c5 during either investigation.

compiled_state.description:
## Impact, stated first

`rebar-autodeploy-review-interrupts` — the paging alarm that bug [rebar:34cd-1a7c-b9b1-4b05] created specifically so the LLM-Review live-lock could never again be invisible — **fired three times in the last seven days**, most recently **2026-08-11T20:05 PDT**, i.e. during the current landing burst. Each firing means an in-flight LLM-Review was killed by a container recreation.

By 34cd design that is the alarm doing its job. The reason it is worth a ticket is that **firing is supposed to be the exceptional case**, reachable (per 34cd) only by "a chronically busy bot" — and three firings in a week says the exceptional case is now routine.

Found by an automated ops error sweep of AWS CloudWatch (account 896586841071, us-east-1) over 2026-08-05T00:00Z -> 2026-08-12T04:00Z. No open ticket covers this; 34cd is closed, and [rebar:9ec0-02b2-8494-4ea5] (in_progress) covers only the *shutdown-side* half — manual restart, reboot, autodeploy rollback — which is a different trigger from the one seen here.

## Occurrences (rebar/host:review_interrupts, Sum > 0)

- 2026-08-07 04:33 PDT
- 2026-08-07 05:55 PDT
- 2026-08-11 20:05 PDT

Alarm state history confirms each as a full OK -> ALARM -> OK episode, self-clearing in ~15 minutes.

## The deferral run-up is the interesting part

`rebar/host:deploy_deferrals` immediately before the 2026-08-11 interrupt:

    2026-08-11 19:00 PDT   11 deferrals
    2026-08-11 20:00 PDT    3 deferrals
    2026-08-11 20:05 PDT    -> review_interrupts = 1

The autodeploy tick is ~2 minutes, so 11 deferrals in the 19:00 hour is roughly 22 minutes of continuous deferring, continuing into the next hour until the interrupt lands. `DEPLOY_DEFER_MAX` is **1800s (30 min)**. The run-up therefore matches the **`bound-exceeded`** path: the bot stayed busy long enough to spend the entire bound, after which autodeploy proceeds and kills the review. The 2026-08-07 firings show the same shape (13 deferrals at 04:00 -> interrupt 04:33; 15 deferrals at 05:00 -> interrupt 05:55).

## Stated uncertainty — this is an inference, not a reading

`rebar/host:review_interrupts` is published with **no dimensions**, so the metric cannot distinguish the two reasons the marker is emitted: `bound-exceeded` (chronically busy) versus `signal-unavailable` (the `/health` `in_flight` signal was unreadable and the deploy proceeded blind). The deferral run-up above is strong circumstantial evidence for `bound-exceeded`, but **confirming it requires `journalctl -u rebar-autodeploy` on the box**, which this sweep did not have access to. That check should be step one.

The distinction matters a great deal, because the two readings imply opposite fixes: `bound-exceeded` means reviews are queueing faster than they complete and the bound is correctly bounding a real overload; `signal-unavailable` means the drain check itself is broken and **every** deploy has been running blind — which would be a silent regression of 34cd rather than its intended behavior.

## Why not just raise DEPLOY_DEFER_MAX

Recording this so it is not the reflexive first move: 34cd chose 1800s deliberately as 1.5x the app-side `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (1200s) ceiling, with a test asserting `bound >= REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` to keep the two in lockstep. Raising it would trade a killed review for a longer deploy stall, and if the true cause is `signal-unavailable` the bound is not involved at all and raising it would change nothing while appearing to.

## Secondary observation, same hour

`rebar/host:mirror_out_of_sync` also recorded a datapoint at 2026-08-11 20:00 PDT (and on 08-04, 08-05, 08-07 x2). These are isolated single datapoints that never breached `rebar-gerrit-mirror-out-of-sync`, so no alarm fired — consistent with brief Gerrit->GitHub replication lag rather than a stuck mirror. Noted for correlation only; not claimed as related.

## Acceptance Criteria

All four are resolved. The disposition is DIAGNOSIS + NO ACTION on autodeploy behaviour;
what remains is carried by two linked child tickets, not by this one.

- [x] The reason field behind each firing is read from `journalctl -u rebar-autodeploy` and
      recorded here: **`bound-exceeded`, all of them** (4 firings, not 3 — see below).
      Read via SSM RunShellScript on i-00880b2c7f13527c5; full evidence in the verdict comment.
- [x] If `signal-unavailable`: **NOT APPLICABLE — ruled out by measurement.** The token appears
      ZERO times in the entire unit journal back to 2026-07-03. 34cd's drain check is healthy
      and has not regressed; the `/health` `in_flight` probe needs no repair.
- [x] If `bound-exceeded`: decision recorded. **A landing burst that outlasts the 30-minute
      bound is ACCEPTED as steady state.** Operator disposition, 2026-08-12: take no action on
      autodeploy behaviour. Do NOT raise `DEPLOY_DEFER_MAX` (34cd pinned it to 1.5x
      `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` under a test, and the saturated trace indicates a larger bound
      would only defer the same kill). Interrupted reviews are retried by the backfill
      reconciler, so this is not an outage. The alarm is firing CORRECTLY on real events.
      Pager-noise retune is deliberately NOT undertaken now: revisit only if the noise becomes
      a problem in practice.
- [x] `review_interrupts` dimensionality: **carried forward, not dropped.** Split out as
      [rebar:613a-e3f4-14a6-45a3] (dowdy-antarctic-junco), linked `discovered_from` this
      ticket. It is observability-only but is a Terraform alarm-contract change requiring an
      operator `terraform apply`, so it is sequenced separately rather than closed here.

## Disposition (2026-08-12)

**Verdict (a): TRUE POSITIVES.** Every firing is a genuine, distinct interrupt; the alarm and
the drain check are both working as designed. Two corrections to this ticket as filed:

1. **There were FOUR firings, not three.** `2026-08-12T03:59:33Z` landed 27 seconds inside the
   sweep's closing boundary and was missed. It came ~56 min after the third, i.e. a second full
   1800s bound spent back-to-back.
2. **The root cause is sharper than "a chronically busy bot".** 34cd justified the 1800s bound
   on the premise that `REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1200` means `in_flight` necessarily reaches 0
   within it. That holds per-review and fails in aggregate: `in_flight` is a CONCURRENT gauge,
   and the episode trace shows it oscillating 2->1->2 across 30 unbroken minutes without ever
   reaching 0. Reviews completed normally throughout; none outlived its timeout. The bound is
   not defeated by a stuck review — it is outlasted by ordinary pipelining. So "reachable only
   by a chronically busy bot" is literally true but does not imply the rarity it was taken to
   imply.

A metric artifact was considered and EXCLUDED by measurement (journal total 7 = offset file 7,
journal intact to 2026-07-03, every datapoint matching a distinct journal line). The latent
rotation double-count hazard found while excluding it is filed as
[rebar:2dc7-31b7-ecbb-4cd2] (affluent-conveyable-dromedary), linked `discovered_from`.

No code was changed, and nothing was mutated on the box or in AWS (read-only `journalctl`,
`cat`, `grep`, and `get-metric-statistics` only).

## Notes

Filed by an automated ops error sweep. No file_impact is recorded and none is expected: the
outcome is a diagnosis plus a recorded no-action decision, with all implementation residue
moved to the two linked child tickets above.
